import perception as P
def summary(env):
    frame = env.frame()
    blobs = [
        (b.color, b.bbox, b.area)
        for b in P.connected_components(frame, min_area=3)
        if b.color != 1
    ]
    print("L6 actions", env.actions, "counts", P.color_counts(frame))
    print("blobs", blobs)
    for action in env.actions:
        clone = env.clone()
        before = clone.frame()
        level = clone.levels_completed
        clone.step(action)
        delta = P.frame_delta(before, clone.frame())
        print(
            "action", action,
            "delta", (delta["count"], delta["bbox"]),
            "reward", clone.levels_completed - level,
            "counts", P.color_counts(clone.frame()),
        )


def probe(env):
    with open("checkpoint.json") as handle:
        prefix = json.load(handle)["final_path"]
    for action in prefix:
        if isinstance(action, list):
            env.step(*action)
        else:
            env.step(action)
    summary(env)


A.run_program("lf52", probe)

def attempted_leaps(env):
    before = pieces(env.frame())
    _, _, bridges, pegs = before
    occupied = bridges | pegs
    found = []
    for source in sorted(occupied):
        for midpoint in sorted(occupied - {source}):
            dr = midpoint[0] - source[0]
            dc = midpoint[1] - source[1]
            if (abs(dr), abs(dc)) not in ((6, 0), (0, 6)):
                continue
            destination = (midpoint[0] + dr, midpoint[1] + dc)
            if not (0 <= destination[0] < 64 and 0 <= destination[1] < 64):
                continue
            clone = env.clone()
            click(clone, source)
            click(clone, destination)
            if pieces(clone.frame()) != before:
                found.append((source, midpoint, destination))
    return found


def selection_context(env):
    _, _, bridges, pegs = pieces(env.frame())
    for label, source in (
        ("bridge", next(iter(bridges))),
        ("peg", min(pegs)),
    ):
        selected = env.clone()
        click(selected, source)
        print(label, "selected", P.frame_delta(env.frame(), selected.frame()))
        for action in (1, 2, 3, 4):
            branch = selected.clone()
            branch.step(action)
            control = env.clone()
            control.step(action)
            a = P.arr(branch.frame()).copy()
            b = P.arr(control.frame()).copy()
            a[0, 0] = b[0, 0]
            print(
                label, "then", action,
                "diff_control", int((a != b).sum()),
                "brief", brief(branch.frame()),
            )

The probe will report only successful transitions and peg-count reductions, avoiding another opaque frame search.

No short key context produced a valid leap, so the obstacle is positional rather than an untested click rule. I’m extending only the key-context frontier and using a dense alignment score: distance between an actual piece and the required midpoint of a visible source-to-hole leap. A score of zero gives a concrete macro to verify.

The expanded run is still within its 600-context cap, but replaying from the staged level makes each context costly. Its output is buffered; if it does not finish on the next poll I’ll stop it and replace replay-per-node with the bounded path-only pattern from `perception.py`.

item.text: The carrier model now explains the prior traces: horizontal keys reposition the carrier while an off-carrier color-8 bridge stays with the world. The missing contexts are therefore “move carrier first, then disembark vertically,” not the reverse order I just scanned. I’m testing those 60 structured placements directly.

A world-coordinate reconstruction exposed the likely corridor: at the seventh carrier column, the color-8 bridge lines up beneath the upper remote board. My previous probe stopped after two upward moves based on the endpoint wall, but at this aligned column it may continue into the board. I’m extending vertical reach there and at adjacent columns.

The aligned upper corridor still blocks entry, so the “carry both pieces” assumption is now suspect. A distinct, cheap branch exists: load only the surviving peg, leave the color-8 bridge on the local board, and move the carrier. I’m testing that configuration before expanding search, because it changes every remote alignment.

item.text: Before attempting pairwise carrier/bridge placements, I’m mapping the bridge’s actual vertical reach at each carrier column. This will tell us whether the lower remote board has an entrance and bounds the next search to reachable rows only.

The reach map revealed the missing context-dependent action: at carrier column 2, repeated Up relocates a color-14 peg from row 42 to row 30 while the color-8 piece stays put. So vertical input is not simply “move the bridge”; it acts on whichever carrier occupant is aligned with an opening. I’m tracing those first four columns turn-by-turn to separate transported-piece motion from newly revealed scenery.

The turn trace exposes a concrete cooperation sequence: at column 2 the peg can climb off the carrier; shift once; at column 3 the bridge can climb beneath it. That creates an adjacent vertical pair and a potential bridge leap into the upper board. I’m verifying this exact macro now before planning beyond it.

The macro is one column left of the upper-board holes: both pieces climb the shaft, but coordinate jumping cannot cross sideways. This now looks like a ladder/docking mechanic rather than peg geometry. I’m testing each key with both pieces staged at the shaft top to see whether horizontal input transfers them onto the board.

The shaft behaves like a one-cell-wide lift: pieces cannot sidestep, but they can be staged in order. The previous order put the bridge below the peg and jammed upward. I’m reversing it—raise the bridge first, bring the carrier’s peg underneath, then push the stack upward—which should place the bridge into the board’s bottom hole if pushing is supported.

The stack cannot push, but it creates a new carrier-transfer opportunity the hole-based macro detector deliberately excluded: the bridge at row 30 can leap downward over the peg at row 36 into the now-empty carrier slot at row 42. I’m testing both directions explicitly; if valid, it lets us swap which carrier slot each piece occupies and changes which remote shaft each can use.

The upper shaft is a dead-end staging lane, so I’m checking its symmetric counterpart at the far-right carrier stop. There, the bridge can climb first; moving the carrier one extra step should align the peg beneath it. This is the untested branch most directly adjacent to the lower remote board.

Both pieces can now be parked off-carrier in the far-right shaft. Horizontal inputs then produce no pixels because they move the empty carrier—a hidden state the earlier frame-key searches collapsed. I’m preserving that action suffix explicitly: move the empty carrier a bounded number of steps, then descend the parked pieces and report only the first changed landing/macro.

The action model is now bounded but the remaining ambiguity is geometric: the shaft ends beside, not inside, the detected peg holes. I’m taking one compact 2× downsampled symbolic map of the remote frame so we can see the walls, carrier track, shafts, and the two remote boards together without dumping the raw 64×64 array.

The symbolic map exposes two special two-cell gate blocks (`?`) at the bottom of the upper board that the peg-hole parser ignored. I’m identifying their raw color and exact component bounds; they are the likely ladder/transfer affordance controlling entry from the carrier shaft.

The ignored gate blocks are color 15—the persistent bridges already modeled by the existing bridge/carrier leg. In the far-right staged state, the movable color-8 piece sits at `(30,28)`, a static bridge is at `(24,28)`, and `(18,28)` is a hole. I’m verifying the direct leap across that bridge; this is the missing connection from the shaft into the upper board.

item.text: After entry, Down separates the carriers: the empty bridge-carrier stops at row 36 while the peg-carrier returns to row 42. That should free the horizontal track for the lower carrier. I’m testing “down, move horizontally, down” to clear the shaft and recycle the empty carrier under the other static gate.

The split works: after one Down, action 3 drives the peg’s lower carrier left while the bridge and its empty carrier stay with the upper world. I’m scanning the finite horizontal stops and pressing Up to find the next shaft where the surviving peg can be raised; this is now a deterministic carrier-routing problem.

The carrier scan now gives an exact upper-board solution. At horizontal stop 3, the peg carrier rises to `(30,28)` directly beneath a static bridge, so it can leap into `(18,28)`. From there a four-macro sequence captures the native upper peg and returns the survivor to the carrier. I’m replaying that full subgoal and checking the peg count after every macro.

The upper subgoal is fully verified: global peg count drops by one and the survivor exits onto its carrier. The movable bridge can remain upstairs; the lower board has two native pegs, so the transported survivor is sufficient to solve it as an ordinary three-peg board. I’m descending that peg carrier and locating the lower-board docking position.

No immediate lower-board capture appears at any horizontal stop, so the survivor carrier is not yet on the lower board’s row/entry. I’m tracing only carrier and peg coordinates while driving right to identify the lower shaft, then I’ll apply the same lift-and-static-bridge pattern used upstairs.

The maze geometry resolves the lower route: the occupied right carrier can climb to row 30 and traverse the horizontal corridor. The earlier probe let it run past intermediate stops without checking macros. I’m rescanning that corridor one stop at a time with a complete move detector that treats color 8 and color 15 as persistent bridge pieces.

The row-30 corridor is definitely the upper-board docking rail, but it may also turn downward into the lower board at one of its horizontal stops. I’m scanning each stop and applying Down stepwise, checking for a new bridge/peg macro after every descent. This directly tests the lower reachability branch the earlier long loops blurred together.

At corridor stop 4 the bridge carrier can descend to row 42 on the far side of the central barrier—this is the first confirmed lower-region reachability. I’m now moving that descended carrier back along the lower corridor and checking every stop for a bridge/peg leap; this is the decisive loop-around-the-wall test.
